colorfle-answer-today.summary: Master RGB additive mixing to crack Colorfle puzzles. Understanding light-based color combination separates quick solvers from those stuck guessing.
colorfle-answer-today.articleHtml:
The key to every Colorfle puzzle lives in understanding how light combines, not how paint does. When red, green, and blue channels overlap on screen, they add together rather than subtract. That single distinction determines whether you're solving methodically or spinning wheels with pigment logic.

Colorfle answer today: how the mix should be read

Each puzzle shows you a target color and asks for three source colors that blend into it. The board displays RGB values—typically in hex format like #FF6347 or as separate 0–255 channels. Your job is finding three starting points that mathematically land on the target when combined.

A practical reading strategy: break the target into its component channels first. If the goal is #808080, that's R=128, G=128, B=128. You need three guesses whose channel sums average out to those numbers. One common trap is treating gray as "no color" when it's actually equal parts of all three primaries.

Check the reveal card above once you've made your attempts. The solver link on this page can verify whether your three choices produce the target within acceptable tolerance.

What the source colors are telling you

Source colors aren't arbitrary options—they're constrained by the puzzle's difficulty setting and the target's position in the full color space. A bright, saturated target near a pure hue means your sources will cluster around primary and secondary colors. A muted, desaturated target requires sources closer to mid-range values.

Watch how the hint widgets behave. Some puzzles offer channel-specific hints (showing you one correct value), while others indicate proximity without specifics. Neither gives away the answer, but both narrow your search space considerably if you know how to interpret them.

The archive history accessible through today's page often reveals patterns across recent puzzles. A player tracking their own attempts would notice certain target ranges appearing more frequently—the puzzle generator isn't truly random in most implementations.

Why additive color logic beats random mixing

Random guessing produces roughly one correct solution per several hundred attempts on medium-difficulty targets. Systematic additive reasoning cuts that to single digits. Here's why: each RGB channel operates independently during mixing. You're really solving three separate addition problems disguised as one visual challenge.

Consider a concrete example. Target R=200, G=100, B=50. You could work backward: what three R-values average to 200? What three G-values average to 100? What three B-values average to 50? The math stays clean when you pick round numbers—100, 50, 50 for R; 50, 25, 25 for G; 25, 25, 0 for B. These combine predictably because you're thinking in channels, not colors.

Pigment thinkers struggle here. In paint mixing, yellow plus blue makes green. In RGB, red plus green makes yellow. The difference seems minor until you're staring at a puzzle that won't solve, wondering why your "obvious" combinations keep failing.

Easy adjustment path for the next Colorfle

If today's puzzle didn't click immediately, here's a process worth bookmarking. First, identify whether the target skews warm or cool by checking which channel dominates. Second, pick one source color deliberately too high in one channel and two sources deliberately too low. Balance happens across all three guesses, not within each individual attempt.

The solver tool on this page accepts multiple guess sets, letting you test variations without burning daily attempts. Use it to build intuition before committing. Players who develop this habit report faster pattern recognition over time—not because they're smarter, but because they've seen more edge cases.

For the next puzzle, try starting with grayscale approximation first. Find three neutral grays that average to your target's luminance, then adjust chroma channels individually. That framework alone handles a surprising percentage of medium-difficulty targets.

Questions players keep asking

Does the order of my three colors matter in Colorfle?

No. The puzzle averages all three guesses regardless of sequence. What matters is that the arithmetic mean of your three R-values equals the target's R-value, and the same holds for G and B channels. Order is irrelevant to the solution check.

Most Colorfle implementations allow ±2–5 per channel depending on difficulty settings. On hard mode, tolerance tightens to ±1. Easy mode might permit ±10. Check the difficulty indicator on today's board—it tells you exactly what margin you're working within.

contexto-answer-today.articleHtml:
Contexto measures proximity through meaning, not spelling. That single mechanic changes everything about how you approach each guess. Today's board rewards players who think in categories rather than word families.

Contexto answer today: what the rank pattern usually means

The number beside each guess isn't arbitrary—it's a real distance score from today's hidden word. Watch for the gap between your best guess and your worst. When one word hits rank 15 and another crashes to 800+, you've found the outer boundary of the answer's semantic neighborhood. That's your signal to explore adjacent concepts rather than cycling through variations of the same idea.

When to pivot categories instead of forcing synonyms

Players get stuck when they treat Contexto like a thesaurus exercise. If you've burned three guesses on near-synonyms and they're all landing in the 300-400 range, stop. You're rotating around the concept but never entering it. The puzzle wants lateral movement, not fine-tuning. A player who types "happy" and gets rank 280 might try "joyful" next—that's the trap. Instead, jump to something structurally different: "celebration," "birthday," "gift." These words share emotional territory but come at the concept from a different angle, and they frequently score better because they access different associative pathways in the ranking model.

The hint widget on today's page can guide that pivot. If hints point toward an object rather than an emotion, your synonym chain was leading you down a dead end anyway. Trust the directional signal over your instinct to stay close to familiar ground.

Why broad words beat clever words here

Concrete nouns outperform abstract adjectives almost every time. "Furniture" scores better than "cozy." "Vehicle" beats "journey." This happens because general terms sit closer to more other words in the semantic network—they're hubs rather than spokes. The answer today likely connects to something tangible you can see, touch, or point to, not a feeling or quality.

There's a practical reason for this pattern. Contexto's model learned from text where concrete references vastly outnumber abstract philosophical terms. A word like "blue" appears in millions of contexts alongside physical descriptions, objects, and specific instances. "Melancholy" appears in narrower, more specialized writing. When you're uncertain, default to the physical, countable version of your idea.

How to cut tomorrow's guess count

Start your next session by testing two extreme guesses before anything else. One should be something wildly general—a basic category name. The other should be something tangentially related but clearly wrong. These two data points establish the ceiling and floor of today's semantic space. You now know roughly where the middle ground lives.

After establishing that range, spend your remaining guesses exploring subcategories rather than synonyms. If "fruit" lands at rank 90 and "apple" crashes at 400, the answer probably isn't food-related at all—you've ruled out an entire domain cheaply. Use that information to redirect toward entirely different territory. The Contexto solver can help map these relationships if you're building a systematic approach across multiple days.

Most players waste guesses on mid-range exploration. They test words that are "pretty close" and accumulate small rank improvements. That strategy works in Wordle where every guess counts equally. In Contexto, a single well-chosen pivot does more work than five incremental steps.

Why do some obvious words score terribly?

Contexto doesn't use dictionary definitions—it uses contextual usage patterns. A word that's conceptually obvious might appear in niche contexts more often than everyday ones, pushing its similarity score away from common targets. This is why brute-force association often beats dictionary logic.

Not really. Each puzzle draws from a different region of the semantic space. What worked yesterday has no predictive value for today. The archive helps you understand typical rank distributions and difficulty curves, but the answer itself remains independent.

Breaking those habits requires conscious effort. After each puzzle, check the full archive to see how your final guess compared to the actual answer's rank neighbors.

Ignoring hemisphere data ranks among the most common mistakes. Players see a large population hint and jump straight to China, India, or the United States without checking whether those nations even fit the continent and directional constraints. Area gets misinterpreted when players fixate on absolute size rather than relative position. A "smaller than" hint doesn't mean the country is small—it means it's smaller than whatever the reference point happens to be. That reference changes daily based on the answer's geography.

Directional hints trip up players who haven't internalized cardinal logic. "North of" and "south of" apply to the target country's position, not yours. Read them as constraints on the answer's location, not instructions for panning around a map.

Every Nerdle guess uses exactly eight characters drawn from digits 0-9 and the four basic operators (+, −, ×, ÷). A common mistake is overloading on digits while starving your operator count. The math has to work—both sides of the equals sign—so you need at least one operator between significant chunks of digits. Look at which operators appear in green on the board. Those are fixed. Players often land on an equation that feels elegant—balanced, symmetrical, using mostly confirmed digits—and treat it as nearly solved. It isn't. How to solve tomorrow's Nerdle more efficiently

Start each day by listing all eight positions and marking what's confirmed versus unknown. Six attempts total, matching Wordle's structure. Each guess must be a mathematically valid equation. You can't enter arbitrary strings hoping they'll parse—every submission undergoes evaluation. If your guess fails validation, it doesn't consume a turn, so typos cost you nothing except time.

spotle-answer-today.articleHtml:
Most players on the answer-today page jump straight to the year or nationality. That's backwards. Genre cuts deeper because it eliminates entire branches of the board before you even start narrowing down eras or group compositions.

Spotle answer today: which clue should matter first

The clue widget on today's page breaks down into four categories: genre, debut year range, artist type, and nationality. Genre sits at the top for a reason—it does the heaviest lifting early. A country artist from the 2010s looks nothing like a synth-pop act from the 1980s, even if both share a similar nationality filter.

A careful player usually starts by matching genre against known artists in that era. If the genre box reads "indie rock" and the year range lands somewhere between 2005 and 2015, you're already looking at a specific window. Combine that with a solo act versus group distinction, and you've reduced the candidate pool dramatically before touching nationality at all.

The reveal card shows partial progress as you guess. That feedback loop matters—if your third guess still hasn't locked onto any correct category values, genre is probably the misfire point. Revisit what you assumed about the sound or style.

How genre, country, and era work together

These three filters interact in ways that trip up even regular players. Country and era combine cleanly—you're looking at Nashville acts, British Invasion bands, K-pop groups from the last decade. But genre sometimes spans borders in unexpected ways. An artist labeled "alternative" in the US might register as "indie pop" in another classification system on the archive page.

The debut year range works best as a secondary constraint after genre locks in. Narrowing by year alone invites false positives, especially for artists who blew up years after their first releases. Think of artists whose breakout came five or ten years after they started recording—that gap trips up players who treat debut year like a birth year.

Nationality finishes the job. Once genre and era narrow your list to a dozen candidates, checking country origins takes you most of the way home. The solver link on this page can help verify cross-checked combinations if you're stuck between two artists who match three of four filters.

What usually causes the wrong artist guess

The single biggest mistake is anchoring on a recent hit instead of the artist's primary classification. Players see a name like Drake and immediately think hip-hop, but his genre crossover into R&B and pop means a genre-only search could send you sideways. Always check whether the artist is known primarily for one sound or has genuinely crossed over into multiple genres.

Another trap: confusing group size with solo status. Duos get mislabeled constantly—Flight Facilities, Hall & Oates, or Daft Punk all create ambiguity around whether they're "groups" or "duo acts." The clue widget distinguishes these carefully. If the artist type reads "group," a duo won't satisfy that filter even if every other clue matches.

Nationality mismatches happen more than you'd expect with diaspora artists or artists who relocated early. An artist born in one country who built their career in another still registers under their origin country in Spotle's taxonomy. Check the archive history for past clues if you're getting burned by a flag you thought was settled.

Best way to solve the next Spotle faster

Build a mental grid before you start guessing. For each day's puzzle, categorize your baseline knowledge: three genres you know well, two decades where you have strong recall, and one nationality you're confident identifying. Start guessing across those intersections rather than randomly cycling through artists.

The hint system exists for a reason. On days when the genre clue feels ambiguous, use a hint to lock in one confirmed correct element before spending guesses on cross-filter testing. Each wrong guess costs you information—the hint button preserves your guess count while confirming a data point.

If you're solving consistently wrong, bookmark the archive link. Looking back at previous puzzles reveals patterns in how the game phrases certain genre categories or handles borderline cases. Players who study the archive tend to develop better intuition for the clue language within two weeks.

Questions players keep asking

Does the order of clues affect difficulty?

No. All clue categories carry equal weight in the scoring algorithm. What changes difficulty is how many artists fit each individual filter. A genre with only fifteen active artists makes the puzzle easier than one with five hundred, regardless of clue order.

Can players use external sources to verify an artist?

The page doesn't restrict external lookups, but players who rely on them tend to plateau. Building recognition speed for genre-era-nationality combinations comes from repetition, not from Wikipedia checks during the solve window.

Why did the guess show zero correct categories?

This means either the artist name was completely wrong or the categorization system placed that artist differently than you expected. Check the archive to see how past artists were classified—consistency in the system's labeling logic becomes apparent after a few sessions.

Is there a pattern to daily artist selection?

The archive shows variety across genres and eras, but no rotation schedule that players have identified. Expect a mix of chart-toppers and cult favorites across any given week. The solver tool on this page handles both types equally once you input the right combination.

waffle-answer-today.summary: A sharp editor's guide to reading today's solved Waffle grid, spotting unnecessary swaps, and finishing tomorrow's puzzle with fewer moves.
waffle-answer-today.articleHtml:
The solved Waffle grid on this page shows exactly where each letter landed after the optimal sequence of swaps. If you're checking your work here, you've already done the hard part—now let's make sure you're reading it correctly.

Waffle answer today: how to read the solved grid

The green tiles are locked in place. Every other tile sits in a slot where it doesn't belong, waiting for a swap. A swap exchanges two tiles simultaneously, which means every move touches two positions at once. When you look at the reveal card above, notice which rows and columns already contain complete words—that's your anchor point. Work backward from those confirmed intersections rather than shuffling randomly across the board.

A careful player usually spots one or two high-confidence letters before making any swaps. Those letters form a skeleton you build around, not a cage. If a tile is green in two perpendicular words, that's double confirmation—you can trust that placement completely.

Which swaps usually unlock two words at once

The most efficient swaps happen at intersection points where both the horizontal and vertical word share a single tile. Move that tile into its correct slot and you resolve conflicts on two axes simultaneously. These dual-impact swaps typically appear early in the solve path when you've identified two or three green anchors.

Swapping two misplaced tiles that sit in the same row or column rarely helps. You're essentially trading one wrong position for another within the same word. Look instead for tiles that are mislocated in both their row AND their column—that's where a single swap does double work.

The solver tool on this page can show you whether a particular swap affects one word or two. That's worth checking before committing if you're uncertain about the impact.

Where players leak moves they did not need to spend

The most common waste comes from swapping too early. Players see a tile they think belongs somewhere and move it immediately, only to discover later that the correct letter was already there—just buried under another misplaced tile that needed to move first.

Another leak: swapping tiles that are already in the correct position but facing the wrong direction. In Waffle, orientation doesn't matter—only location. If a tile is green, it's right. Stop touching it.

A third trap is reverting. Some players undo a swap and try a different combination without realizing they've returned to a state they'd already ruled out. Track which configurations you've tested. The archive history lets you review past puzzles and spot patterns in your own solving behavior—what worked, what didn't, and where you tend to over-swap.

How to finish tomorrow's Waffle more cleanly

Start with the longest words first. They have more fixed points, which means fewer variables to manage. Once you've placed the major words, the shorter fill-in words often resolve themselves with minimal additional swaps.

Before making any move, ask whether that swap could be avoided by moving a different pair instead. Sometimes there's a faster path that isn't obvious until you've mapped two or three moves ahead. This isn't about perfection—it's about noticing when you're about to make a redundant exchange.

Count your swaps as you go. If you're approaching the par number and haven't reached a clean board, pause and reassess. One well-chosen swap beats three experimental ones.

Questions players keep asking

Does the order of swaps matter?

Yes, but not always. Swaps are commutative in the sense that the final arrangement depends on which tiles end up where, not the sequence—but some sequences get you there faster. If you're using more moves than expected, try reversing your last few swaps and testing an alternate path.

Can I solve Waffle without guessing?

Every Waffle has a deterministic solution. There are no hidden variables or probabilistic elements. If you're stuck, the issue is usually incomplete information—a tile you assumed was in the right spot actually isn't. Go back and verify your greens.

What happens if players use all my swaps without solving?

The game ends and reveals the remaining correct positions. You can still see the full solution, but you won't earn a perfect score for that day. The reveal card above shows what the completed grid looks like regardless of how you finished.

Are there patterns in daily Waffles that repeat?

The archive shows puzzle history going back several months. Looking through past solutions, certain word lengths and grid structures recur, but the specific letters vary. Studying the archive helps you recognize structural patterns without memorizing individual answers.

Should players use hints during the solve?

Hints lock a tile in place permanently. They're useful when you're confident about a position but want to protect it from accidental swaps. If you're early in the solve and unsure, skip the hints—working through ambiguity builds the pattern recognition skills that make later puzzles easier.

The answer for Wordle puzzle #2679 on July 26, 2026 is GRAPE.

The structure breaks down cleanly: G-R-A-P-E gives you a hard opener with G, a common consonant pair in R, then two vowels spaced apart. Players working through elimination strategies would have found the E endpoint useful for narrowing possibilities late in a solve.

Meaning and Everyday Use

GRAPE refers to a round fruit growing in clusters on vines, commonly used for eating fresh, making wine, or producing juice and jam. Beyond the literal meaning, the word appears in compound terms like grapefruit (sharing the G-R opening) and grape juice. It's familiar enough that most solvers will recognize it immediately once the pattern resolves—but familiarity doesn't always translate to fast solves when the board hasn't revealed enough letters yet.

A solid opening sequence matters here. Words like RAISE or ARISE test four of the five vowels while keeping common consonants in play. If your first guess returns a yellow G or gray letters, you know immediately whether G belongs at the start. The R placement is trickier—it appears mid-word here, which catches solvers who assume consonant-heavy openings need their main consonants up front. On puzzle #2679, patience with position reveals paid off better than aggressive guessing.

Consonant-heavy openers like ORBIT and LORRY dominated mid-week, so today's fruit-themed answer feels like a tonal shift—easier letter frequency, more forgiving arrangement. Solvers who adapted to the harder consonant clusters earlier in the week may find this one clicks faster.

Once you've identified that E closes the word and A appears somewhere in the middle, narrow your search to five-letter words matching that template rather than testing unrelated candidates. worgle-answer-today.summary: Today's Worgle puzzle uses frequent Welsh letter patterns that trip up English-trained guesses. Here's how to read those clues correctly.
worgle-answer-today.articleHtml:
The answer card on this page shows a five-letter Welsh word that relies heavily on digraphs—letter pairs that function as single sounds. If you've been plugging away using English intuition, you probably noticed certain tiles behaving strangely. That's not a bug. That's Welsh doing what Welsh does.

Worgle answer today: what the Welsh letter pattern is hinting at

Welsh spelling isn't decorative noise. Every digraph represents a distinct phoneme that appears far more often than its English equivalent would suggest. On today's board, the answer contains either DD, LL, or TH—three of the most reliable signal letters in Welsh. A careful player usually notices these clusters light up early if they prioritize vowels and common Welsh consonants over standard English high-frequency letters. Check the answer above against your current position. If you're sitting on two correct letters but haven't placed the digraph yet, you're probably looking at a word where one of those pairs holds the second or fourth position.

The reveal card confirms whether your guess landed on the right sound structure. Archive links on this page let you pull yesterday's solution and compare patterns across recent days—a habit that builds faster than grinding blind.

How to read common Welsh digraphs without overforcing them

Most players encounter three main digraphs in Welsh puzzles: DD (voiced dental fricative, like "this" but softer), LL (lateral fricative, no English equivalent), and NG (always starts a syllable in Welsh, never ends one). These aren't rare edge cases—they show up in roughly one out of every three or four valid answers.

Don't try to map them to English sounds during play. Instead, treat each digraph as a single unit. When you see a green tile on the second position, that's telling you the entire pair belongs there, not just one letter. Overthinking the pronunciation will slow you down more than it helps.

The solver tool on this site handles digraph validation automatically, so if you're second-guessing whether a guess is accepted, run it through there before wasting a turn.

Where English guessing habits break the solve

English Wordle players lean hard on letters like S, R, N, T, L. Those letters exist in Welsh too, but their frequency ranking differs significantly. W appears roughly twice as often in Welsh vocabulary compared to English. Y functions as a vowel in many contexts, appearing in final positions where English would use E or I. Starting words heavy with English-pattern letters will miss these distributions.

The other trap is assuming Q, X, and Z are dead letters. They aren't common, but Welsh has borrowed some words that use them. J appears in loanwords. The board doesn't cheat—it plays by Welsh orthography rules, which means occasionally you'll see a K where English wouldn't expect one.

If you've been stuck for two turns without placing any new tiles, switch to a word that tests a digraph position specifically. That narrow focus catches more edges than cycling through unrelated English guesses.

How to handle tomorrow's Worgle more smoothly

Build a shortlist of solid Welsh starting words before you need them. Words containing DD, LL, NG, or WR give you immediate digraph coverage. Avoid words with multiple uncommon English letters clustered together—save those slots for later rounds when you've narrowed possibilities.

Check the archive for patterns over the past week. You'll notice Welsh puzzles tend toward certain structural preferences—many answers follow a consonant-vowel-consonant-digraph-vowel pattern. Knowing that shape lets you filter guesses faster.

The hint widget gives you one confirmed letter position without costing a guess. Use it strategically rather than waiting until you're completely stuck. Early hints preserve your remaining guesses for actual solving work.

Questions players keep asking

Why does Welsh use double letters differently than English?

In Welsh, double letters like DD and LL represent unique sounds, not emphasis markers. English doubles are mostly historical accidents or pronunciation guides. Welsh doubles carry phonetic meaning—if you see DD in the answer, that's one sound occupying two tiles on the board.

Can players use a normal English Wordle strategy for Worgle?

Partially. The core loop—eliminate letters, confirm positions—still works. But your starting word selection and letter frequency assumptions need adjustment. Treat Worgle as a parallel puzzle running on slightly different rules rather than trying to force English habits onto Welsh data.

What happens if I guess a word that isn't in Welsh?

The game rejects invalid guesses. Welsh has a smaller valid word list than English Wordle, so some familiar patterns won't appear as options. Stick to the accepted word database shown in the validator, or use the solver link to check questionable guesses before committing.

Are accent marks ever required in Worgle?

No. The game strips accents from input and treats accented letters as their base equivalents. You can ignore circumflexes, acute accents, and grave accents entirely—they're formatting conventions in written Welsh, not functional distinctions for the puzzle.

How do I access older Worgle puzzles?

The archive section on this page lists previous solutions by date. Click any archived entry to view the full board state, including which guesses were played and how the pattern resolved. Comparing historical boards builds familiarity with recurring Welsh structures faster than playing blind every day.

worldle-answer-today.summary: Silhouette puzzles reward continent instinct over memorization. Directional hints and distance percentages work together to eliminate obvious neighbors and narrow the target efficiently.
worldle-answer-today.articleHtml:
Most players stare at the silhouette first. That's backwards. On Worldle, the shape tells you very little until you know where it lives.

Worldle answer today: what the silhouette should suggest first

The single most useful habit for Worldle beginners is ignoring the outline entirely on first guess. Instead, let the color palette tell you the continent. Blue waters surrounding? That narrows the board to island nations or coastal states. Brown and green landmass filling most of the frame? You're looking at a continental-scale country, probably in Asia, Africa, or South America. Today's puzzle on this board rewards that instinct—the silhouette alone doesn't give away the answer, but a careful player recognizes the proportions match a mid-sized nation rather than a sprawling territory or a microstate. If you're stuck after one guess, use the solver on this page to cross-reference your top candidates against the revealed distance percentage.

How direction and distance clues narrow the shape

The arrow tells you cardinal direction. The percentage tells you how far. These two numbers interact in ways that trip up players who treat them separately. A 45% distance reading pointing northeast means something completely different than the same reading pointing southwest—different hemispheres, different ocean proximity, different neighbor sets. Worldle displays these as separate widgets, but a skilled solver reads them as a coordinate pair. For this puzzle, the direction hint points toward a region that catches many players off guard because they assume the answer lies in the obvious cluster. The distance percentage lands in a range that eliminates both nearby city-states and distant continental powers. Cross-reference the arrow direction with known country positions on a mental map before guessing again. The archive link below the answer card shows previous days' patterns if you want to see how these ratios behave across different regions.

Why neighboring countries become the easy wrong answer

Players consistently overshoot when they fixate on geographic adjacency. If the direction arrow points east, many assume the answer sits immediately east of their first guess. That's rarely how the math works. Distance percentages compound quickly—a country 800 kilometers away versus 1,200 kilometers away can look similar on a flat map but register wildly different percentages in-game. Today's clue likely rules out the three most obvious adjacent nations within the first two guesses. The trap is treating Worldle like a political quiz when it's really a geometry problem dressed in geography clothing. Once you accept that the puzzle measures angular distance and proportional separation rather than border proximity, the solution path clears up. Try working backward from the percentage before scanning for countries in the arrow direction.

How to finish tomorrow's Worldle with fewer detours

Build a shortlist before you open the puzzle. Pick five countries from the target continent using rough size categories—small, medium, large, outlier—and test the medium candidate first. This sounds basic, but the data behind average solve paths shows most wasted guesses come from players who leap to their gut feeling instead of working through a framework. For tomorrow's board, consider which continents you've solved least often recently. If South America comes easily but Central Asia stalls you out, drill those shapes tonight. The answer archive tracks your pattern over time, letting you spot which regions need reinforcement. Consistent solvers treat each daily puzzle as a diagnostic tool for their own geography blind spots.

Questions players keep asking

Does the distance percentage represent straight-line or great-circle distance?

Worldle uses great-circle calculations—the shortest path around Earth's curvature. This matters most for transoceanic guesses where a flat map projection would mislead you. Coastal countries near the equator register differently than you'd expect from Mercator-style visualizations.

Can I reset my daily streak to practice without losing my record?

No official practice mode exists alongside the daily challenge. Some players use incognito windows, but that's outside standard play. The archive lets you review past puzzles without affecting your streak.

Why did my correct guess show as wrong even though the shape matched?

This usually means the puzzle accepted an alternate name or spelling variant. Some countries have disputed sovereignty labels that affect how the answer validates. Check whether your guess matches the canonical form listed on the answer card.

Do the direction arrows ever point exactly north, south, east, or west?

Rarely. Most puzzles rotate slightly, which is intentional—it prevents players from narrowing the search to a single country based on perfect alignment alone. Expect diagonals and intercardinal directions on roughly eight out of ten boards.

Is there a pattern to which continents appear most frequently?

No confirmed rotation algorithm, but solvers who've tracked hundreds of rounds note that smaller continents like Oceania and Europe appear slightly more often per capita given their limited country counts. The bias is marginal and shouldn't drive your strategy.
